summary:
Kerala stands under India's national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist; the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers sexual orientation and gender identity under Article 15; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 Sakshi Jain, an openly transgender law student, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Kerala's own enforcement record under the national Act is among the highest sub-national totals in India, though the underlying national counts are very small. A Queerbeat crime-data report of 30 January 2026 records 2 of the 7 national cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 in Kerala, and 4 of the 11 in 2023, a figure joint-highest with Tamil Nadu; the report cautions that national totals are tiny because of police-registration bias.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Kerala's position in the national enforcement data is illustrative rather than exceptional in kind. The same Queerbeat compilation shows only 7 cases registered nationally under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 11 in 2023, so Kerala's share of 2 and 4 respectively reflects a very small denominator, and the report attributes low national figures to police-registration bias rather than an absence of violence.

The welfare machinery a trans visitor may encounter in Kerala sits within a wider state-level pattern: Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha maintain comparable transgender welfare boards, so board-based access to pensions, housing subsidies and public-hospital surgery is a regional norm rather than a Kerala-specific provision.

Regional judicial protections are unevenly distributed. The Madras High Court's April 2019 order banning sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants binds Tamil Nadu, not Kerala, and its 2021 S. Sushma guidelines were issued by that court; whether equivalent directions have been issued for Kerala is not addressed in the sources.

Document and checkpoint friction is documented at transport hubs and airports across India rather than in Kerala specifically, including Chennai International Airport in November 2024 and railway stations in Kolkata and Assam, so screening risk should be expected at national points of entry as well as within the state.
localsOnly:
Kerala is among the 12 states and union territories reported to Parliament in December 2021 as having constituted a Transgender Welfare Board under Section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Rules, 2019, per a federal press information release.

The Kerala board coordinates state-level benefits of the kind delivered by the Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra and Odisha boards: housing subsidies, sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions for transgender residents.

Transition-related healthcare for members of the transgender community is covered nationally under the Ayushman Bharat scheme following its expansion in April 2024, which residents can draw on alongside state board provision.

Since August 2024 the Ministry of Finance has confirmed that LGBTQ people face no legal restriction on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries, a resident-facing entitlement unaffected by the March 2026 narrowing of recognition.

Residents also fall under Article 15 protections against discrimination on grounds including sex as interpreted by the Supreme Court to cover gender identity, and under the Allahabad High Court's 2021 extension of that protection to employment on sexual-orientation grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2026 amendment's narrowed recognition scheme changes eligibility for Kerala's existing welfare-board benefits, or for Ayushman Bharat coverage, is unresolved in the sources available here.

Police-conduct findings are drawn from national and other-state material: the UK country policy note of December 2025 and the June 2024 detainee interviews are not Kerala-specific, and no Kerala-specific police-abuse dataset is sourced.

The Queerbeat figures for Kerala are small enough that year-to-year movement cannot be read as a trend, and the report's own caveat on police registration means unreported incidents are not captured; the split between offences reported under the Act and other charges is not broken out.

Whether conversion therapy continues to operate in Kerala despite the Madras High Court ban of 7 June 2021 and the National Medical Commission's 2022 ban is not sourced; the evidence of clandestine networks is national.

The practical effect of the 2026 amendment on entry, visa and document screening for a visitor whose identity documents do not match the recognised categories is not addressed in any source listed here.
